ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Favaloro Foundation Only participants who met these criteria and provided informed consent were included in the study.

To evaluate the incremental validity of the PFS beyond established measures of eating-related constructs, a hierarchical regression analysis was conducted predicting binge approval number CBE 940/21) and was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Favaloro Foundation Only participants who met these criteria and provided informed consent were included in the study.

Participants were excluded if Spanish was not their native language (n = 6, 0.72%), if they reported being in the postpartum or lactation period (n = 3, 0.36%), or if implausible anthropometric values were detected, including irregular responses for height (n = 5, 0.60%) or weight (n = 3, 0.36%).
Participants completed an ad hoc sociodemographic questionnaire assessing age, sex, educational level, weight, height, and hormonal cycle characteristics.
Upon accessing the survey, participants were presented with an informed consent form outlining the study's objectives and the voluntary nature of participation.
To minimize missing data, all questions were mandatory, and participants were required to complete the questionnaire in a single session, as enforced by the survey platform settings.
First, participants completed the informed consent and a sociodemographic questionnaire.

Participants were adults living in Argentina, recruited through social media using a snowball strategy; 73% were women, 40.1% had completed secondary education, and 34.1% had university education; race and ethnicity were not recorded, so we cannot examine how cultural, socioeconomic, and structural factors related to them shape hedonic hunger.
Participants were recruited through various social media platforms using a nonprobabilistic snowball sampling strategy.
Participants were recruited through announcements disseminated on various social media platforms, including WhatsApp, Instagram, LinkedIn, and Reddit.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding

32 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, **5 were flagged *only* by short-scale straightlining** (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

**What this does not cover.** Only 1 of 53 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

reproducibility_check.title: Reproducibility Check
reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 2 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).
-  1 of 2 scripts ran without error when executed.
-  25 installable dependencies detected.
- 232 statistics stored from the extracted output; 19 of 127 reported tests matched (15%).

ethics_statements: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Favaloro Foundation Only participants who met these criteria and provided informed consent were included in the study.

To evaluate the incremental validity of the PFS beyond established measures of eating-related constructs, a hierarchical regression analysis was conducted predicting binge approval number CBE 940/21) and was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
live_data_statements: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Favaloro Foundation Only participants who met these criteria and provided informed consent were included in the study.

Participants were excluded if Spanish was not their native language (n = 6, 0.72%), if they reported being in the postpartum or lactation period (n = 3, 0.36%), or if implausible anthropometric values were detected, including irregular responses for height (n = 5, 0.60%) or weight (n = 3, 0.36%).
Participants completed an ad hoc sociodemographic questionnaire assessing age, sex, educational level, weight, height, and hormonal cycle characteristics.
Upon accessing the survey, participants were presented with an informed consent form outlining the study's objectives and the voluntary nature of participation.
To minimize missing data, all questions were mandatory, and participants were required to complete the questionnaire in a single session, as enforced by the survey platform settings.
First, participants completed the informed consent and a sociodemographic questionnaire.

Participants were adults living in Argentina, recruited through social media using a snowball strategy; 73% were women, 40.1% had completed secondary education, and 34.1% had university education; race and ethnicity were not recorded, so we cannot examine how cultural, socioeconomic, and structural factors related to them shape hedonic hunger.
Participants were recruited through various social media platforms using a nonprobabilistic snowball sampling strategy.
Participants were recruited through announcements disseminated on various social media platforms, including WhatsApp, Instagram, LinkedIn, and Reddit.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 2 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:2, File = c("1-Script analisis indices.R", 
"2-Analisis_psicometrico_revisado.R"), "Runs after" = c("—", 
"1-Script analisis indices.R"), Basis = c("numeric", "dependency"
)), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

**2 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `1-Base_cruda_final.xlsx` to `../Databases/1-Base_cruda_final.xlsx` (in 1-Script analisis indices.R); `2-Base_Indices.xlsx` to `../Databases/2-Base_Indices.xlsx` (in 2-Analisis_psicometrico_revisado.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 2 scripts: 1 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.
**`setwd()` in the code**

**2 scripts call `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.
Reproducible after removing `setwd()`: 2-Analisis_psicometrico_revisado.R.
**Calls that install packages in the code**

4 calls to `install.packages()`, `groundhog`, `checkpoint`, `renv`, `pacman` and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: `groundhog.library()` and `p_load()` by `library()`, the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.

> get_cut <- function(x, y){
>   r  <- roc(y, x, levels = c(0, 1), direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)
>   co <- as.data.frame(coords(r, "best", best.method = "youden",
>           ret = c("threshold", "sensitivity", "specificity"), transpose = FALSE))
>   c(auc  = as.numeric(auc(r)),
>     thr  = as.numeric(co[1, "threshold"]),
>     sens = as.numeric(co[1, "sensitivity"]),
>     spec = as.numeric(co[1, "specificity"]))
> }
> cv_cut <- function(x, y, k = 10, reps = 100){
>   res <- matrix(NA_real_, reps, 3, dimnames = list(NULL, c("sens", "spec", "thr")))
>   for(r in seq_len(reps)){
>     fold <- integer(length(y))
>     for(cl in unique(y)){
>       idx <- which(y == cl)
>       fold[idx] <- sample(rep(seq_len(k), length.out = length(idx)))   # folds estratificados
>     }
>     TP <- FN <- TN <- FP <- 0
>     thr <- numeric(k)
>     for(f in seq_len(k)){
>       tr     <- fold != f
>       thr[f] <- get_cut(x[tr], y[tr])["thr"]            # corte derivado SOLO en entrenamiento
>       pred   <- x[!tr] > thr[f]
>       obs    <- y[!tr] == 1
>       TP <- TP + sum(pred & obs);   FN <- FN + sum(!pred & obs)
>       TN <- TN + sum(!pred & !obs); FP <- FP + sum(pred & !obs)
>     }
>     res[r, ] <- c(TP / (TP + FN), TN / (TN + FP), mean(thr))
>   }
>   res
> }
> roc_validate <- function(x, y, etiqueta, B = 2000, k = 10, reps = 100){
>   ok <- complete.cases(x, y); x <- x[ok]; y <- y[ok]
>   full <- get_cut(x, y)
>   boot <- t(replicate(B, { i <- sample(length(y), replace = TRUE); get_cut(x[i], y[i]) }))
>   ci   <- apply(boot, 2, quantile, probs = c(.025, .975), na.rm = TRUE)
>   cv   <- cv_cut(x, y, k = k, reps = reps)
>   data.frame(
>     Criterio        = etiqueta,
>     n = length(y), n_positivos = sum(y == 1),
>     AUC             = round(full["auc"], 3),
>     AUC_boot_IC     = sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]", ci[1, "auc"],  ci[2, "auc"]),
>     Corte_muestra   = round(full["thr"], 3),

>     Sens_CV         = round(mean(cv[, "sens"]), 3),

>     Score_Observado = score,

text.text: The Power of Food Scale (PFS) measures hedonic hunger, the motivation to eat palatable food in the absence of energy need, and, to our knowledge, no Spanish-language validation had been reported.

We adapted the PFS into Spanish and evaluated it as a transdiagnostic, dimensional measure in 810 community-dwelling adults in Argentina (73.3% women, mean age 39 years; race and ethnicity were not recorded).
Using split-sample exploratory factor analysis, we identified three factors.
In contrast, the correlated three-factor model fit marginally in confirmatory analysis (CFI = .90, TLI = .88, RMSEA = .09).

A bifactor model fit well (CFI = .96, RMSEA = .07); the general factor explained 71% of the common variance (ωH = .84), supporting interpretation of the total score, but subscale scores carried little unique reliable variance (ωS = .16-.31).
Reliability was high (α = .915, ω = .934), and invariance across sex held within conventional thresholds.

Scores correlated strongly with hedonic eating, binge-eating symptoms, and bulimic symptoms and discriminated binge-eating severity groups (AUC = .86; exploratory cutoff = 3.03, crossvalidated sensitivity = .81, specificity = .74).

However, discriminant validity relative to a related measure of hedonic overeating was not established (HTMT = .89), incremental validity was minimal, and equivalence with the English version was not tested.

The total score of the Spanish-language PFS appears to be a reliable index of hedonic hunger across the severity of binge-eating and eating-disorder symptoms in Argentine adults; subscale use, clinical applications, and cross-language equivalence require further study.

Beyond its biological function, eating behavior is strongly shaped by socioemotional, sensory, and psychological factors that influence food choice and consumption (Gibson, 2006; Macht & Simons, 2000).
text.formatted: Beyond its biological function, eating behavior is strongly shaped by socioemotional, sensory, and psychological factors that influence food choice and consumption <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Gibson, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Macht & Simons, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: In modern food environments, characterized by the widespread availability of highly palatable, energy-dense, and ultra-processed foods, eating is increasingly driven by pleasure rather than by physiological hunger.
Researchers have conceptualized this phenomenon as hedonic hunger, defined as the motivation to consume palatable foods despite no energy deprivation (Cameron et al., 2014; Lowe & Butryn, 2007).
text.formatted: Researchers have conceptualized this phenomenon as hedonic hunger, defined as the motivation to consume palatable foods despite no energy deprivation <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Cameron et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Lowe & Butryn, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Hedonic hunger is closely linked to food's rewarding properties, including taste, texture, smell, and appearance, which generate positive hedonic evaluations and reinforce consumption (McCrickerd & Forde, 2016; Rogers et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Hedonic hunger is closely linked to food's rewarding properties, including taste, texture, smell, and appearance, which generate positive hedonic evaluations and reinforce consumption <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(McCrickerd & Forde, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Rogers et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Foods high in sugar and fat elicit particularly strong reward responses, activating dopaminergic circuits involved in motivation and reinforcement, and promoting intake even when energy needs are met (Volkow et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Foods high in sugar and fat elicit particularly strong reward responses, activating dopaminergic circuits involved in motivation and reinforcement, and promoting intake even when energy needs are met <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Volkow et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Through learning and conditioning, repeated exposure to these foods strengthens associations between environmental cues and reward, potentially weakening inhibitory control and fostering maladaptive eating patterns (Reichelt et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Through learning and conditioning, repeated exposure to these foods strengthens associations between environmental cues and reward, potentially weakening inhibitory control and fostering maladaptive eating patterns <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Reichelt et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: In contemporary societies where highly rewarding foods are ubiquitous, individual sensitivity to food reward may become maladaptive (Volkow et al., 2011).
text.formatted: In contemporary societies where highly rewarding foods are ubiquitous, individual sensitivity to food reward may become maladaptive <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Volkow et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Food-related cues interact with individual differences in reward sensitivity and impulsivity, increasing vulnerability to overeating (Price et al., 2015; Witt & Lowe, 2014).
text.formatted: Food-related cues interact with individual differences in reward sensitivity and impulsivity, increasing vulnerability to overeating <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Price et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Witt & Lowe, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Food reactivity can occur without actual consumption, manifesting as persistent thoughts and desires related to food (Cappelleri et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Food reactivity can occur without actual consumption, manifesting as persistent thoughts and desires related to food <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Cappelleri et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: These processes are particularly relevant in binge eating, where individuals experience recurrent episodes of excessive food intake accompanied by a subjective loss of control, often involving highly palatable foods and occurring independently of physiological hunger (American Psychiatric Association, 2013).
text.formatted: These processes are particularly relevant in binge eating, where individuals experience recurrent episodes of excessive food intake accompanied by a subjective loss of control, often involving highly palatable foods and occurring independently of physiological hunger <ref type="bibr">(American Psychiatric Association, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Evidence suggests that prior restriction of palatable foods may further enhance their salience, reinforcing impulsive consumption patterns (Hagan et al., 2003; Oswald et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Evidence suggests that prior restriction of palatable foods may further enhance their salience, reinforcing impulsive consumption patterns <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Hagan et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Oswald et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Parallels have been drawn between these eating behaviors and substance use disorders, as both involve heightened cue reactivity, craving, and difficulties in inhibitory control (Di Segni et al., 2014; Franken, 2003).
text.formatted: Parallels have been drawn between these eating behaviors and substance use disorders, as both involve heightened cue reactivity, craving, and difficulties in inhibitory control <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Di Segni et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Franken, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: These theoretical and empirical developments have increased interest in reliable instruments that capture individual differences in hedonic responsiveness to food environments.

The most widely used instrument for assessing hedonic hunger is the Power of Food Scale (PFS; Lowe et al., 2009), which measures susceptibility to the hedonic aspects of the food environment across three food proximity levels: food available, food present, and food tasted.
text.formatted: The most widely used instrument for assessing hedonic hunger is the Power of Food Scale (PFS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Lowe et al., 2009)</ref>, which measures susceptibility to the hedonic aspects of the food environment across three food proximity levels: food available, food present, and food tasted.

text.text: The 15-item abbreviated version (Cappelleri et al., 2009) uses a 5-point Likert scale.
text.formatted: The 15-item abbreviated version <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Cappelleri et al., 2009)</ref> uses a 5-point Likert scale.

text.text: Original validation showed high internal consistency (α = .91) and strong associations with disinhibition, emotional eating, and binge eating (Espel-Huynh et al., 2018; Lowe et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Original validation showed high internal consistency (α = .91) and strong associations with disinhibition, emotional eating, and binge eating <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Espel-Huynh et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Lowe et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: The PFS has since been validated in Japanese (Yoshikawa et al., 2012), Portuguese (Ribeiro et al., 2015), German (Andreeva et al., 2019), Iranian (Aliasghari et al., 2020), and Italian (Torelli et al., 2022) populations, demonstrating cross-cultural robustness.
text.formatted: The PFS has since been validated in Japanese <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Yoshikawa et al., 2012)</ref>, Portuguese <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Ribeiro et al., 2015)</ref>, German <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Andreeva et al., 2019)</ref>, Iranian <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Aliasghari et al., 2020)</ref>, and <ref type="bibr">Italian (Torelli et al., 2022)</ref> populations, demonstrating cross-cultural robustness.

text.text: Hedonic responsiveness to food is not specific to a single diagnosis.

It has been linked to binge eating, bulimic and other eating-disorder symptoms, overeating, and higher body weight (Andreeva et al., 2019; Lowe et al., 2009; Torelli et al., 2022), which makes it a candidate dimension for transdiagnostic assessment across the severity continuum of eating pathology.
text.formatted: It has been linked to binge eating, bulimic and other eating-disorder symptoms, overeating, and higher body weight <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Andreeva et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Lowe et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Torelli et al., 2022)</ref>, which makes it a candidate dimension for transdiagnostic assessment across the severity continuum of eating pathology.

text.text: Despite these advances, no validated Spanish version of the PFS is currently available, and research on hedonic hunger remains scarce in Latin American contexts.

In Argentina, empirical work has primarily focused on the prevalence of eating disorders and associated risk factors, such as dietary restraint and binge eating, without explicitly examining the role of hedonic motivation in food consumption (Gómez-Peresmitré et al., 2013; Rutsztein et al., 2010 Rutsztein et al., , 2021)).
text.formatted: In Argentina, empirical work has primarily focused on the prevalence of eating disorders and associated risk factors, such as dietary restraint and binge eating, without explicitly examining the role of hedonic motivation in food consumption <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Gómez-Peresmitré et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Rutsztein et al., 2010</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Rutsztein et al., , 2021))</ref>.

text.text: This gap is particularly relevant given the high prevalence of disordered eating behaviors reported in the country and the growing public health burden associated with overeating and loss of control, and the increasing exposure to highly palatable and ultra-processed foods across multiple contexts -including social media, advertising, and digital media -which may amplify hedonic responsiveness and complicate regulatory efforts (Monteiro et al., 2019; UNICEF, 2023).
text.formatted: This gap is particularly relevant given the high prevalence of disordered eating behaviors reported in the country and the growing public health burden associated with overeating and loss of control, and the increasing exposure to highly palatable and ultra-processed foods across multiple contexts -including social media, advertising, and digital media -which may amplify hedonic responsiveness and complicate regulatory efforts <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Monteiro et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">UNICEF, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, this study aimed to adapt the PFS into Spanish and to evaluate its psychometric properties as a transdiagnostic, dimensional measure in an Argentine community sample.

Specifically, we examined its structure (split-sample exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, bifactor indices), reliability, measurement invariance across sex, item functioning with item response theory, convergent and discriminant validity, its gradient across the severity of binge-eating and eating-disorder symptoms, and exploratory cutoffs and regression-based norms.
This study's design and its analyses were not preregistered; some analyses were added in response to editorial feedback and are labeled exploratory.
The de-identified data and the analysis code are available at https://osf.io/crn7b/.
text.formatted: The de-identified data and the analysis code are available at <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/crn7b/">https://osf.io/crn7b/</ref>.

text.text: The Spanish version of the PFS is not publicly available because the original instrument is copyrighted by Drexel University (see Method); some other instruments described in the Method (e.g., the EDI-3) are commercially published and are not shared.

Data were analyzed using R, version 4.6.1 (R Core Team, 2026) and the packages lavaan (version 0.7.3; Rosseel et al., 2026), psych (version 2.6.9; Revelle, 2026), mirt (version 1.48; Chalmers, 2012), pROC (version 1.19.1; Robin et al., 2011), NormData (version 1.2; Van der Elst, 2026), nortest (version 1.0.4; Gross & Ligges, 2015), and car (version 3.1.5; Fox & Weisberg, 2019).
text.formatted: Data were analyzed using R, version 4.6.1 <ref type="bibr">(R Core Team, 2026)</ref> and the packages lavaan (version 0.7.3; <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Rosseel et al., 2026)</ref>, psych (version 2.6.9; <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Revelle, 2026)</ref>, mirt <ref type="bibr">(version 1.48;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Chalmers, 2012)</ref>, pROC (version 1.19.1; <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Robin et al., 2011)</ref>, NormData (version 1.2; <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Van der Elst, 2026)</ref>, nortest (version 1.0.4; <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Gross & Ligges, 2015)</ref>, and car (version 3.1.5; <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Fox & Weisberg, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Favaloro Foundation Only participants who met these criteria and provided informed consent were included in the study.
A total of 833 individuals completed the survey.

Participants were excluded if Spanish was not their native language (n = 6, 0.72%), if they reported being in the postpartum or lactation period (n = 3, 0.36%), or if implausible anthropometric values were detected, including irregular responses for height (n = 5, 0.60%) or weight (n = 3, 0.36%).
Potential duplicate entries were screened by examining IP address, submission time, and key demographic variables (age, sex, and body measures).
Only cases showing highly similar responses across multiple indicators were considered likely duplicates and removed (n = 4, 0.48%).
One participant was excluded due to an implausible age value (n = 1, 0.12%).
Finally, a participant was excluded for being below the minimum age eligibility criterion (n = 1, 0.12%), yielding a final sample of 810 participants.
The final analytical sample (N = 810) ranged in age from 18 to 84 years (M = 39.00, SD = 15.61), with a mean BMI of 25.50 (SD = 5.56).
The sample was predominantly female (73.3%).
Most participants reported completing secondary (40.1%) or university education (34.1%).
Most followed an omnivorous diet (88.1%), and most were not currently dieting (67.8%).
To avoid overfitting, the sample was randomly divided into two equal subsamples (random seed = 123, n = 405 each; Hopwood & Donnellan, 2010).
text.formatted: To avoid overfitting, the sample was randomly divided into two equal subsamples (random seed = 123, n = 405 each; <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Hopwood & Donnellan, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: EFA was conducted on the first subsample and CFA on the second subsample.
All remaining analyses (convergent validity, known-groups comparisons, IRT, measurement invariance, normative data) were conducted on the full sample.
Participants completed an ad hoc sociodemographic questionnaire assessing age, sex, educational level, weight, height, and hormonal cycle characteristics.
BMI was calculated from self-reported height and weight (Hosseini & Padhy, 2020).
text.formatted: BMI was calculated from self-reported height and weight <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Hosseini & Padhy, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The adaptation of the PFS (Lowe et al., 2009)  Content validity was evaluated by the four expert judges, who received a spreadsheet describing the construct and the evaluation criteria.
text.formatted: The adaptation of the PFS <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Lowe et al., 2009)</ref>  Content validity was evaluated by the four expert judges, who received a spreadsheet describing the construct and the evaluation criteria.

text.text: They rated each item from 1 (not adequate at all) to 5 (very adequate) on semantic clarity, grammatical correctness, cultural relevance, and appropriateness for the educational and developmental level of Argentine adults, and could add qualitative comments.
The Content Validity Index (CVI) of each item was computed following Lawshe (1975), and items with CVI > .78 were considered adequate.
text.formatted: The Content Validity Index (CVI) of each item was computed following <ref type="bibr">Lawshe (1975)</ref>, and items with CVI > .78 were considered adequate.

text.text: The Argentine Spanish adaptation of the Power of Food Scale (PFS) used in this study is not publicly available for download, as the original instrument is copyrighted by Drexel University.
Researchers interested in accessing or using the Power of Food Scale or any of its adaptations should contact Dr.
Michael R. Lowe directly at lowe@drexel.edu to request permission under the terms of the applicable copyright and trademark licenses.
The Power of Food Scale is a self-report instrument designed to assess the psychological impact of living in food-rich environments with easy access to highly palatable foods.
Unlike measures focused on actual food consumption, the PFS assesses appetite and hedonic responsiveness to food, independent of homeostatic hunger.

The present study used the 15-item abbreviated version of the PFS (Cappelleri et al., 2009), which retains the original three-factor structure based on food proximity: food available, food present, and food tasted.
text.formatted: The present study used the 15-item abbreviated version of the PFS <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Cappelleri et al., 2009)</ref>, which retains the original three-factor structure based on food proximity: food available, food present, and food tasted.

text.text: Items are rated on a 5-point scale ranging from 1 (do not agree at all) to 5 (strongly agree), with higher scores indicating greater hedonic responsiveness to the food environment.
Subjective appetite was assessed using the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), a recommended primary control measure in appetite research (Dakin et al., 2026; Flint et al., 2000; Parker et al., 2004).
text.formatted: Subjective appetite was assessed using the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), a recommended primary control measure in appetite research <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Dakin et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Flint et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Parker et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: The VAS measures subjective sensations related to eating behavior using 100-mm horizontal lines on which participants indicate the intensity of each sensation at the time of assessment.

The following items were included: hunger ("How hungry do you feel right now?"), desire to eat ("How strong is your desire to eat right now?"), fullness ("How full do you feel right now?"), Moreover, prospective food consumption ("How much do you think you could eat right now?").
Scores were obtained by measuring the distance in millimeters from the left anchor, yielding values ranging from 0 to 100.
A composite appetite score was calculated using the following formula: Appetite score = (Hunger + Desire to eat + (100 -Fullness) + Prospective food consumption) / 4.
Higher scores reflect greater subjective appetite.
The
Eating behavior was further assessed using the revised 18-item Three-Factor Eating Questionnaire (de Lauzon-Guillain et al., 2006; Stunkard & Messick, 1985).
text.formatted: Eating behavior was further assessed using the revised 18-item Three-Factor Eating Questionnaire (de <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Lauzon-Guillain et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Stunkard & Messick, 1985)</ref>.

text.text: This self-report instrument evaluates three dimensions of eating behavior: cognitive restraint, uncontrolled eating, and emotional eating.
Items are rated on a 4-point response scale, and separate scores are calculated for each dimension, with higher scores indicating greater levels of the respective eating behavior.
The Spanish version of the Three-Factor Eating Questionnaire (Vázquez-Velázquez et al., 2022) showed good internal consistency (α = .86).
text.formatted: The Spanish version of the Three-Factor Eating Questionnaire <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Vázquez-Velázquez et al., 2022)</ref> showed good internal consistency (α = .86).

text.text: Binge eating symptoms were assessed using the Binge Eating Scale (BES) (Gormally et al., 1982), in a version currently being validated for use in the Argentine population (Pedrón et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Binge eating symptoms were assessed using the Binge Eating Scale (BES) <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Gormally et al., 1982)</ref>, in a version currently being validated for use in the Argentine population <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Pedrón et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The BES consists of 11 items with graded-response options that assess behavioral, cognitive, and emotional aspects of binge eating.
The total score is obtained by summing item responses, along with two domain scores reflecting behavioral/motivational and emotional components.
Higher scores indicate greater severity of binge eating symptoms and allow classification into low, moderate, and high levels according to established cut-off points.
The Binge Eating Scale (BES) total score demonstrated good reliability (α = .88) in this sample.

Hedonic overeating was assessed using the Hedonic Overeating Questionnaire (Hilbert et al., 2022) (HEDO-Q), a brief self-report measure designed to evaluate trait-like hedonic overeating and loss-of-control overeating.
text.formatted: Hedonic overeating was assessed using the Hedonic Overeating Questionnaire <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Hilbert et al., 2022)</ref> (HEDO-Q), a brief self-report measure designed to evaluate trait-like hedonic overeating and loss-of-control overeating.

text.text: The original version of the HEDO-Q has demonstrated good internal consistency (α = .82) and adequate construct validity, distinguishing between individuals with and without obesity and eating disorders.
In the present study, an Argentine version currently undergoing validation was used (Serafini et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In the present study, an Argentine version currently undergoing validation was used <ref type="bibr">(Serafini et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This version consists of six items grouped into three subscales: Liking (items 3 and 5), Wanting (items 1 and 4), and Loss of control (items 2 and 6).
Items are rated on a 5-point scale ranging from 0 (never) to 4 (always).
A total score is computed by averaging the six items, with higher scores indicating greater hedonic overeating.
The HEDO-Q total scale showed good internal consistency (α = .87).
Eating disorder-related psychopathology was assessed using the Eating Disorder Inventory-3 (Garner, 2004).
text.formatted: Eating disorder-related psychopathology was assessed using the Eating Disorder Inventory-3 <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Garner, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: It comprises 91 items organized into 12 primary subscales.

Three of these subscales constitute the Eating Disorder Risk Scales (Drive for Thinness, Bulimia, and Body Dissatisfaction), while the remaining nine assess general psychological traits of clinical relevance, such as Low Self-Esteem, Perfectionism, and Interoceptive Deficits.
Items are rated on a 6-point Likert scale.

Responses indicating the absence of symptoms are scored as 0, whereas the four options reflecting increasing symptom severity are scored 1-3, with higher values corresponding to greater psychopathology.
The EDI-3 has shown adequate internal consistency, with Cronbach's alpha coefficients typically exceeding .80 across its primary scales.
Locally, several linguistic and conceptual adaptations of the EDI have been conducted across successive versions (Casullo & Pérez, 2003; Rutsztein et al., 2006 Rutsztein et al., , 2013)).
text.formatted: Locally, several linguistic and conceptual adaptations of the EDI have been conducted across successive versions <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Casullo & Pérez, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Rutsztein et al., 2006</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Rutsztein et al., , 2013))</ref>.

text.text: The Eating Disorder Inventory (EDI) subscales in the current sample showed generally good internal consistency.
Specifically, Drive for Thinness (α = .88), Bulimia (α = .87), and Body Dissatisfaction (α = .89) showed good reliability, while Low Self-Esteem (α = .90) reached excellent levels.
Personal Alienation (α = .83), Interpersonal Insecurity (α = .84), Interpersonal Distrust (α = .86), and Emotional Dysregulation (α = .82) also demonstrated good internal consistency.

Interoceptive Awareness (α = .79), Perfectionism (α = .75), and Maturity Fears (α = .76) showed acceptable reliability, whereas Asceticism (α = .69) presented slightly lower, though still acceptable, internal consistency.
Upon accessing the survey, participants were presented with an informed consent form outlining the study's objectives and the voluntary nature of participation.
No monetary compensation was provided.
To minimize missing data, all questions were mandatory, and participants were required to complete the questionnaire in a single session, as enforced by the survey platform settings.
The survey consisted of five sections presented in a fixed initial order followed by randomized questionnaires.
First, participants completed the informed consent and a sociodemographic questionnaire.
Next, they completed the Power of Food Scale, the Hedonic Overeating Questionnaire, the Intuitive Eating Scale-2, the Three-Factor Eating Questionnaire, and the Eating Disorder Inventory-3.
The order of these questionnaires was randomized for each participant to control potential order effects.
Prior to the analyses, the dataset was screened for completeness and adherence to inclusion criteria.
Cases with more than 10% missing responses on the target scale were excluded, and the remaining missing data were minimal and handled with pairwise deletion.
Item responses were scored following each instrument's original procedures.

A total mean score was computed rather than a sum score to facilitate cross-study comparisons and to maintain interpretability on the original 1-5 response scale, consistent with prior PFS validations (Cappelleri et al., 2009; Lowe et al., 2009).
text.formatted: A total mean score was computed rather than a sum score to facilitate cross-study comparisons and to maintain interpretability on the original 1-5 response scale, consistent with prior PFS validations <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Cappelleri et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Lowe et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Descriptive statistics were calculated for each PFS item (mean, median, standard deviation, minimum, maximum, and percentage of missing responses).
Item distributions were inspected with skewness and kurtosis and tested with the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test with the Lilliefors correction.

Corrected item-total correlations were computed to evaluate each item's contribution to the total score, and an item intensity index estimated the degree of endorsement relative to the theoretical response range.
The sample was randomly divided into two equal subsamples (n = 405; random seed = 123).

In the first subsample, sampling adequacy was assessed with the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin index and Bartlett's test of sphericity, and an exploratory factor analysis (EFA) was run with maximum-likelihood extraction and oblimin rotation; the number of factors was determined with parallel analysis, eigenvalues, and the scree plot.
In the second subsample, confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) tested the threefactor model of the original validation and a bifactor model (one general factor and three orthogonal specific factors).
Because item distributions deviated from normality, models were estimated with robust maximum likelihood (MLR), which provides scaled fit statistics.
Fit was assessed using the χ² statistic, CFI, TLI, RMSEA (90% CI), and SRMR, and the two models were compared using these indices.

From the bifactor model, we computed omega total (ωT), omega hierarchical (ωH), omega for each specific factor (ωS), the explained common variance (ECV), the percentage of uncontaminated correlations (PUC), and the average relative parameter bias (ARPB; Reise et al., 2013; Rodriguez et al., 2016).
text.formatted: From the bifactor model, we computed omega total (ωT), omega hierarchical (ωH), omega for each specific factor (ωS), the explained common variance (ECV), the percentage of uncontaminated correlations (PUC), and the average relative parameter bias (ARPB; <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Reise et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Rodriguez et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Reliability.
Cronbach's α and split-half reliability were computed for the total scale and each subscale in the full sample (N = 810).
McDonald's ω was computed from the standardized loadings of the CFA models in the second subsample.
Invariance across biological sex was tested with multigroup CFA (configural, metric, and scalar models) in the full sample, using ΔCFI ≤ .010 and ΔRMSEA ≤ .015 as criteria (Cheung & Rensvold, 2002).
text.formatted: Invariance across biological sex was tested with multigroup CFA (configural, metric, and scalar models) in the full sample, using ΔCFI ≤ .010 and ΔRMSEA ≤ .015 as criteria <ref type="bibr">(Cheung & Rensvold, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Items were also analyzed with a graded response model (GRM; Samejima, 1969), which yields discrimination (a) and threshold (b) parameters.
text.formatted: Items were also analyzed with a graded response model (GRM; <ref type="bibr">Samejima, 1969)</ref>, which yields discrimination (a) and threshold (b) parameters.

text.text: Discrimination was classified as high (a ≥ 1.70), moderate (0.65-1.70), or low (< 0.65; Baker, 2001).
text.formatted: Discrimination was classified as high (a ≥ 1.70), moderate (0.65-1.70), or low (< 0.65; <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Baker, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Item fit was evaluated with the S-χ² statistic (Orlando & Thissen, 2000), and test and item information curves were examined to identify the range of the latent trait where the scale is most precise.
text.formatted: Item fit was evaluated with the S-χ² statistic <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Orlando & Thissen, 2000)</ref>, and test and item information curves were examined to identify the range of the latent trait where the scale is most precise.

text.text: Convergent and discriminant validity.
Convergent validity was examined with Spearman correlations with false discovery rate (FDR) correction.

Discriminant validity with respect to the HEDO-Q was evaluated with the heterotrait-monotrait ratio (HTMT; Henseler et al., 2015; bootstrap 95% CI, 2,000 resamples), with latent correlations between the PFS factors and the HEDO-Q tested against 1 with scaled χ² difference tests (Anderson & Gerbing, 1988; Rönkkö & Cho, 2022), and with the correlation between total scores corrected for attenuation.
text.formatted: Discriminant validity with respect to the HEDO-Q was evaluated with the heterotrait-monotrait ratio (HTMT; Henseler et al., 2015; bootstrap 95% CI, 2,000 resamples), with latent correlations between the PFS factors and the HEDO-Q tested against 1 with scaled χ² difference tests <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Anderson & Gerbing, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Rönkkö & Cho, 2022)</ref>, and with the correlation between total scores corrected for attenuation.

text.text: Known-groups validity.
PFS scores were compared across binge-eating severity groups defined with the Binge Eating Scale (BES).

Normality and homogeneity of variances were checked with the Shapiro-Wilk and Levene tests; because the assumptions were not met, we used Kruskal-Wallis tests (effect size ε²) with Bonferroni-corrected pairwise Wilcoxon tests.

Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses used two criteria: the high-severity BES group (versus low and moderate) and, exploratorily, scores at or above the 75th percentile of the Eating Disorder Risk Composite Preliminary normative data.
Regression-based normative data were derived following Corvalán et al. (2026) and Van der Elst (2024).
text.formatted: Regression-based normative data were derived following <ref type="bibr">Corvalán et al. (2026)</ref> and <ref type="bibr">Van der Elst (2024)</ref>.

text.text: A linear regression model predicted PFS total scores from age, sex, BMI, and their interactions, and stepwise backward elimination based on the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) retained age (mean-centered), biological sex, BMI, and an age × sex interaction.

Residuals from the final model were standardized and converted to percentile ranks using the empirical cumulative distribution, allowing an individually adjusted percentile for any combination of these variables.
Descriptive percentile reference values (5th, 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th, 90th, and 95th) were also computed for the total sample and by age group.

Generative AI (Claude, Anthropic; Sonnet and Opus models accessed through claude.ai) was used to support the development and debugging of the analysis code in R, to suggest analytic approaches, and to edit the language of the manuscript.
De-identified item-level survey data were shared with the tool.
The authors chose the analyses, ran all code, checked the outputs against the R console results, and reviewed and edited all text.
Four expert judges evaluated content validity using the CVI (Lawshe, 1975).

In the second subsample (n = 405), the correlated threefactor model showed marginal fit: χ² (87) = 380.27, p < .001; CFI = .90; TLI = .88; RMSEA = .091, 90% CI [.082, .101]; SRMR = .068.

text.text: Internal consistency was high for the total score (α = .915; ω = .934; split-half = .946).
For the subscales, α was .868 (Food Available), .854 (Food Present), and .778 (Food Tasted), and ω was .873, .855, and .757.
The α and split-half coefficients were computed in the full sample (N = 810), and ω was computed from the CFA models in the second subsample.
Measurement invariance of the PFS was examined using a sequential confirmatory approach comparing configural, metric, and scalar models across biological sex.
The configural model showed acceptable fit (CFI = .91, RMSEA = .09), confirming that the same factor structure was supported in both men and women.
The transition to the metric model resulted in a negligible change in fit (ΔCFI = -.002, ΔRMSEA = -.002, p = .069), supporting the equality of factor loadings across groups (metric invariance).
The scalar model showed a further small decrease in fit (ΔCFI = -.003, ΔRMSEA = -.001), with the chi-square difference test reaching statistical significance (p = .002).

Although this formally indicates scalar non-invariance, the magnitude of fit deterioration remained well below conventional thresholds (ΔCFI ≤ .010; ΔRMSEA ≤ .015; Cheung & Rensvold, 2002), suggesting that measurement properties of the PFS are substantially equivalent across biological sex.

text.text: Item discrimination parameters (a) ranged from 0.77 to 3.06 (M = 1.84, SD = 0.59).
Most items showed moderate to high discrimination.
Specifically, 11 of 15 items yielded discrimination parameters of 1.70 or higher, indicating high sensitivity to individual differences in hedonic hunger.
Four items showed comparatively lower discrimination: PFS9 (a = 0.77), PFS14 (a = 0.96), PFS15 (a = 1.07), and PFS10 (a = 1.58).

The item with the lowest discrimination in the IRT analyses (PFS9, a = 0.77) corresponded to the item with the lowest corrected item-total correlation in the CTT analyses (r = .37), confirming its comparatively weaker contribution to measurement precision.
Item fit indices (S-χ²) were non-significant for 12 of 15 items, indicating adequate model-data fit.
Three items showed marginally significant misfit (PFS1, PFS5, PFS9; all ps < .05), though RMSEA values for these items remained small (≤ .021).

text.text: The test information curve showed that the PFS provides maximum measurement precision in the range of θ ≈ -1 to 2, suggesting the scale is most informative for individuals with low to moderately elevated hedonic hunger -which is theoretically consistent with its development in non-clinical community samples.

The comparatively lower discrimination observed for PFS9 and PFS14 aligns with their position in the Food Tasted subscale, which may tap more salient eating behavior rather than motivational susceptibility to food cues.

text.text: PFS scores showed strong positive correlations with hedonic eating measures, including liking (ρ = .70), wanting (ρ = .70), and dyscontrol (ρ = .59).

Significant positive associations were also observed with uncontrolled eating (ρ = .65), emotional eating (ρ = .48), binge eating symptoms (ρ = .62), drive for thinness (ρ = .36), and body dissatisfaction (ρ = .31).

Negative correlations emerged with intuitive eating dimensions, including reliance on hunger and satiety cues (ρ = -.37), body-food choice congruence (ρ = -.17), physical reasons for eating (ρ = -.36), and emotional reasons for eating (ρ = -.52).
No significant association was found with cognitive restraint (ρ = .05, p = .198).
Small but significant positive correlations were observed with pre-exposure hunger (ρ = .22) and post-exposure hunger (ρ = .28; Table 2).

text.text: Discriminant validity with respect to the HEDO-Q was not established.
The HTMT ratio between the PFS and the HEDO-Q was .89 (95% CI [.86, .92]), above the .85 criterion and with an upper limit above .90.

Latent correlations with the HEDO-Q were .91 (95% CI [.88, .95]) for Food Available, .75 [.70, .80] for Food Present, and .75 [.69, .80] for Food Tasted; all were statistically different from 1 (scaled χ² differences = 32.0, 174.5, and 144.0, df = 1, ps < .001; Table 3).

text.text: We examined associations between PFS scores and sociodemographic variables, including age, biological sex, body mass index (BMI), educational level, dieting status, and hormonal cycle phase.
PFS scores were negatively associated with age (ρ = -.29, p < .001) and positively associated with BMI (ρ = .21, p < .001).

text.text: Consistent with the convergent validity analyses, PFS scores were positively associated with both pre-exposure and post-exposure hunger ratings, suggesting that trait-level hedonic responsiveness is related to momentary hunger-related states.
PFS scores discriminated the high binge-eating severity group (BES) from the rest of the sample (AUC = .86, bootstrap 95% CI [.82, .89]).

The cutoff that maximized Youden's index was 3.03 (bootstrap 95% CI [2.70, 3.37]), with sensitivity = .81 and specificity = .75; in 10-fold cross-validation, with the cutoff derived in the training folds, sensitivity was .81 and specificity .74.

For the exploratory EDI criterion (scores at or above the 75th percentile of the Eating Disorder Risk Composite in this sample), the AUC was .77 (95% CI [.73, .81]); the cutoff was 2.77 (bootstrap 95% CI [2.37, 3.17]), with apparent sensitivity = .77 and specificity = .65, and cross-validated values of .77 and .65 (Figure 2; Table S10).

text.text: This study adapted the Power of Food Scale (PFS) into Spanish.

It evaluated its psychometric properties in a community sample of 810 adults in Argentina, to examine it as a transdiagnostic, dimensional measure of hedonic hunger across the severity continuum of binge-eating and eating-disorder symptoms.

The evidence supports interpreting the total score: reliability was high, a bifactor structure with a dominant general factor fit well, and scores were strongly related to hedonic eating, binge-eating symptoms, and bulimic symptoms.

Evidence for the subscales and for discriminant validity relative to a closely related measure was weaker, and clinical applications remain to be tested in clinical samples and against diagnostic interviews.
The three-factor model showed marginal fit in the confirmation subsample (CFI = .90, TLI = .88, RMSEA = .09).
In contrast, the bifactor model fit well (CFI = .96, RMSEA = .07).

Because bifactor models tend to fit better than correlated-factors models, the bifactor indices are more informative: the general factor accounted for 71% of the common variance, ωH was .84, and ignoring the specific factors biased the general-factor loadings by only 5%.
With these values, interpreting the total score as an essentially unidimensional index is justified (Reise et al., 2013; Rodriguez et al., 2016).
text.formatted: With these values, interpreting the total score as an essentially unidimensional index is justified <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Reise et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Rodriguez et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: By contrast, the specific factors explained little reliable variance once the general factor was controlled (ωS = .16, .23, and .31), so subscale scores should be interpreted with caution.

This is consistent with prior validations supporting the three-factor structure (Aliasghari et al., 2020; Andreeva et al., 2019; Ribeiro et al., 2015; Torelli et al., 2022; Yoshikawa et al., 2012) while suggesting that most of the reliable variance in the PFS reflects a single dimension.
text.formatted: This is consistent with prior validations supporting the three-factor structure <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Aliasghari et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Andreeva et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Ribeiro et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Torelli et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Yoshikawa et al., 2012)</ref> while suggesting that most of the reliable variance in the PFS reflects a single dimension.

text.text: The subscale-level differences should be read in this light.
Food Available and Food Present showed stronger associations with binge-eating severity (ε² = .375 and .329; AUC = .880 and .840) than Food Tasted (ε² = .101; AUC = .683).
This pattern is compatible with the distinction between anticipatory wanting and consummatory liking (Berridge & Robinson, 2016).
text.formatted: This pattern is compatible with the distinction between anticipatory wanting and consummatory liking <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Berridge & Robinson, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: However, two measurement features offer an alternative reading: Food Tasted had the lowest reliability (ω = .76), and the items with the weakest loadings on the general factor (PFS9, PFS14, and PFS15; λ = .33-.45) attenuate its correlations.
Food Tasted also retained the largest specific variance (ωS = .31), mainly through PFS9 (specific loading = .82), so a distinct taste-focus component may exist.
However, this needs confirmation in independent samples before making differential interpretations.

Measurement invariance across biological sex was supported at the metric level, and the scalar model stayed within conventional thresholds (ΔCFI = -.003), so scores can be compared between women and men.

Equivalence with the English-language original was not tested, and the adaptation relied on a single forward translation without independent backtranslation, so it remains unknown whether the Spanish and English versions are measurement-equivalent.

Convergent validity was strong: PFS scores correlated with hedonic eating (ρ = .59-.70), uncontrolled and emotional eating (ρ = .65 and .48), and bulimic symptoms (ρ = .62), and negatively with intuitive eating dimensions (ρ = -.17 to -.52), in line with accounts of hedonic hunger as sensitivity to food reward (Lowe & Butryn, 2007; McCrickerd & Forde, 2016) and with frameworks distinguishing cue-triggered motivation from interoceptive regulation (Dakin et al., 2025; Lopez & Cruz-Vespa, 2022).
text.formatted: Convergent validity was strong: PFS scores correlated with hedonic eating (ρ = .59-.70), uncontrolled and emotional eating (ρ = .65 and .48), and bulimic symptoms (ρ = .62), and negatively with intuitive eating dimensions (ρ = -.17 to -.52), in line with accounts of hedonic hunger as sensitivity to food reward <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Lowe & Butryn, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">McCrickerd & Forde, 2016)</ref> and with frameworks distinguishing cue-triggered motivation from interoceptive regulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Dakin et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Lopez & Cruz-Vespa, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The near-zero association with cognitive restraint (ρ = .05) supports divergence from dietary restraint.

However, discriminant validity relative to the HEDO-Q was not established: latent correlations were high (r = .75 for Food Present and Food Tasted, .91 for Food Available), the HTMT was .89 (95% CI [.86, .92]), and the correlation between total scores corrected for attenuation was about .90.
Although a correlation of 1 was statistically rejected, the two instruments overlap substantially and may largely index the same construct.
The strongest EDI-3 correlation emerged with the bulimia scale (ρ = .62), followed by drive for thinness (ρ = .36) and body dissatisfaction (ρ = .31).

This graded pattern is consistent with the transdiagnostic view that hedonic responsiveness to food cues is most closely tied to loss-of-control eating, with smaller links to the weight-and shape-related symptom domains (Andrade et al., 2024; Andreeva et al., 2019; Di Segni et al., 2014; Franken, 2003; Lowe et al., 2009).

text.text: The PFS added a statistically significant but very small amount of explained variance in binge-eating severity beyond age, BMI, uncontrolled and emotional eating, and the HEDO-Q (ΔR² = .007), which, given the overlap with the HEDO-Q, indicates little unique predictive information.

The two instruments are better seen as largely overlapping indicators of hedonic responsiveness than as measures of different constructs; comparing them directly in the same sample against prospective outcomes (e.g., loss-of-control eating, treatment engagement, weight change) is a priority for future research (Hilbert et al., 2022; Howard et al., 2021; Schreyer et al., 2023).

text.text: PFS scores increased across binge-eating severity groups with a large effect (ε² = .35), and discrimination of the high-severity group was good (AUC = .86, 95% CI [.82, .89]).
A cutoff of 3.03 had sensitivity = .81 and specificity = .75 in the full sample, with nearly identical cross-validated values (.81 and .74), but a wide bootstrap interval (2.70-3.37).

These estimates should be treated as exploratory: both the PFS and the BES are self-reports, the BES severity groups were not validated against a diagnostic interview, and the EDI-based analysis (AUC = .77; cutoff = 2.77) used the 75th percentile of the same sample as the criterion, so it indicates only that higher PFS scores accompany higher symptom levels in this sample.

PFS scores predicted post-questionnaire hunger beyond baseline hunger and BMI, and this association was moderated by baseline hunger, consistent with an interactionist view in which hedonic responsiveness is expressed according to the momentary physiological context (Belfort-DeAguiar & Seo, 2018; Lowe & Butryn, 2007).
text.formatted: PFS scores predicted post-questionnaire hunger beyond baseline hunger and BMI, and this association was moderated by baseline hunger, consistent with an interactionist view in which hedonic responsiveness is expressed according to the momentary physiological context <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Belfort-DeAguiar & Seo, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Lowe & Butryn, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Because food exposure was operationalized as questionnaire completion, hunger changes are descriptive indices rather than cue-reactivity outcomes.
PFS scores decreased with age and increased with BMI, and no sex differences emerged, in line with the invariance results indicating that scores can be compared between women and men.

Associations with dieting status and hormonal cycle category agree with evidence that restriction increases food cue salience and that endocrine context influences hedonic responsiveness (Arnoni-Bauer et al., 2017; Hagan et al., 2003; Oswald et al., 2011; Swales et al., 2023).

text.text: Given the convenience sampling strategy, these norms should be considered preliminary.
The findings may not generalize beyond the studied sample.

Participants were adults living in Argentina, recruited through social media using a snowball strategy; 73% were women, 40.1% had completed secondary education, and 34.1% had university education; race and ethnicity were not recorded, so we cannot examine how cultural, socioeconomic, and structural factors related to them shape hedonic hunger.

The sample was non-clinical, and symptoms were self-reported, so the results may not apply to people with diagnosed eating disorders or to other Spanish-speaking countries, where food environments and language use differ.
Replication in clinical samples, in other Spanish-speaking countries, and in more diverse samples is needed.
Several limitations should be acknowledged.

First, the adaptation relied on a single forward translation by a certified translator, reviewed by two authors, without independent back-translation, and we did not test measurement equivalence with the English-language original, so it remains unknown whether the two versions function equivalently.

Second, the sample was non-clinical, predominantly female (73.3%), recruited online through snowball sampling, and limited to adults in Argentina, which restricts representativeness (see Constraints on Generality).

Third, all measures were self-reports, open to social desirability, recall bias, and differences in introspective accuracy, and no diagnostic interview was used; the binge-eating severity groups and the eating-disorder composite therefore indicate symptom levels, not diagnoses, and the cutoffs derived from them are exploratory and imprecise.
Fourth, the criterion for the EDI-based analysis was the 75th percentile of the same sample, so it reflects relative standing in this sample rather than clinical risk.

Fifth, the correlated three-factor model fit only marginally; the specific factors explained little reliable variance, and the PFS overlapped substantially with the HEDO-Q, limiting interpretation of subscale scores and the scale's distinctiveness from related measures.
Sixth, we had no testretest data, so temporal stability is unknown.
Seventh, food exposure was operationalized only as questionnaire completion rather than a standardized cue paradigm, so changes in hunger are descriptive indices, not cue-reactivity outcomes.
Finally, the cross-sectional design precludes conclusions about predictive validity.

In sum, the Spanish-language PFS showed high reliability and a dominant general factor in Argentine adults, supporting the interpretation of its total score as an index of hedonic hunger that varies along the severity continuum of binge-eating and eating-disorder symptoms.
Evidence for subscale scores and for discriminant validity relative to the HEDO-Q was limited.

Future research should test the equivalence of the Spanish and English versions, examine the scale in clinical samples and against diagnostic interviews, include test-retest and prospective designs, and compare the PFS directly with the HEDO-Q (Burger & Stice, 2011; Lowe & Butryn, 2007).

text.text: Four independent experts assessed each item for semantic clarity and grammatical adequacy, as well as the appropriateness of its difficulty relative to the target population's educational and developmental level.
For semantic clarity and grammatical correctness, 13 of the 15 items had a CVI of 1.00, indicating full agreement among experts.
Two items yielded a CVI of 0.50, reflecting partial agreement.
Experts subsequently reviewed and refined these items based on qualitative feedback, making specific modifications to improve lexical precision and clarity.

Regarding item difficulty relative to the educational and developmental level of the Argentine adult population, all items had a CVI of 1.00, indicating unanimous expert agreement on the appropriateness of the language used.
Overall, these findings support the content validity of the adapted scale and meet Lawshe's (1975) criteria.

Because PFS scores were associated with age, age-stratified percentile estimates were also examined.
Median PFS scores were highest in the younger age groups and decreased progressively with increasing age.

Specifically, the median (P50) was 2.87 in participants aged 18-25 years, 2.87 in those aged 26-35 years, 2.60 in those aged 36-45 years, 2.20 in those aged 46-60 years, and 2.13 in those aged 61 years and older.
A similar age-related gradient was observed across the upper percentiles.

These findings are consistent with the negative association observed between age and PFS scores and provide preliminary descriptive reference values for future research and potential clinical interpretation.

text.text: Item discrimination parameters (a) ranged from 0.77 to 3.06 (M = 1.84, SD = 0.59).
Most items showed moderate to high discrimination.
Specifically, 11 of 15 items yielded discrimination parameters of 1.70 or higher, indicating high sensitivity to individual differences in hedonic hunger.
Four items showed comparatively lower discrimination: PFS9 (a = 0.77), PFS14 (a = 0.96), PFS15 (a = 1.07), and PFS10 (a = 1.58).

The item with the lowest discrimination in the IRT analyses (PFS9, a = 0.77) corresponded to the item with the lowest corrected item-total correlation in the CTT analyses (r = .37), confirming its comparatively weaker contribution to measurement precision.
Item fit indices (S-χ²) were non-significant for 12 of 15 items, indicating adequate model-data fit.

The PFS total score showed strong positive correlations with hedonic eating measures, including liking (ρ = .70), wanting (ρ = .70), and dyscontrol (ρ = .59).
Significant positive associations were also observed with uncontrolled eating (ρ = .65), emotional eating (ρ = .48), binge eating symptoms (ρ = .62), drive for thinness (ρ = .36).
Body dissatisfaction (ρ = .31).

Negative correlations were observed with several intuitive eating dimensions, including reliance on hunger and satiety cues (ρ = -.37), body-food choice congruence (ρ = -.17), physical reasons for eating (ρ = -.36), and emotional reasons for eating (ρ = -.52).
No significant association was found with cognitive restraint (ρ = .05, p = .198).

text.text: The Food Available subscale showed the strongest associations with HEDO Dyscontrol (ρ = .62), emotional eating (ρ = .53), drive for thinness (ρ = .41), and cognitive restraint (ρ = .13).
In contrast, these associations were weaker or non-significant for the Food Tasted subscale.
Conversely, the Food Tasted subscale showed comparatively attenuated negative associations with intuitive eating dimensions.
These differential patterns are compatible with partially distinct aspects of hedonic food motivation.
However, given the low reliable specific variance of the subscales (see the main manuscript), they should be interpreted with caution.
These findings support the scale's convergent validity.

text.text: To further explore the theoretical relationship between trait hedonic responsiveness and momentary hunger, regression analyses were conducted predicting post-exposure hunger ratings.

In a model controlling for baseline hunger and BMI, PFS scores significantly predicted post-exposure hunger (B = 3.29, SE = 0.56, t = 5.88, p < .001), whereas BMI did not significantly predict post-exposure hunger.

text.text: An interaction model further showed a significant interaction between PFS scores and baseline hunger (B = 0.08, SE = 0.02, t = 3.41, p < .001), indicating that the association between trait hedonic responsiveness and postexposure hunger varied with baseline hunger.

text.text: Finally, exploratory analysis examining the joint pattern of PFS, binge eating severity, and hedonic eating dimensions showed that PFS scores were strongly associated with both binge eating severity (ρ = .63) and hedonic eating dimensions, especially liking (ρ = .70) and wanting (ρ = .70).
The strongest association within this profile emerged between binge eating severity and hedonic dyscontrol (ρ = .72), suggesting a coherent hedonic vulnerability pattern across related constructs.

Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses evaluated the ability of PFS scores to discriminate the high binge-eating severity group (BES) from the rest of the sample.
The PFS showed good discriminative performance, with an area under the curve (AUC) of .86 (bootstrap 95% CI [.82, .89]).

The cutoff that maximized Youden's index was 3.03 (bootstrap 95% CI [2.70, 3.37]), yielding a sensitivity of .81 and a specificity of .75; in 10-fold crossvalidation, with the cutoff derived in the training folds, sensitivity was .81 and specificity .74 (Table S10).

The process had five steps: (a) a certified public translator produced a forward translation into Spanish; (b) two authors reviewed it for linguistic and conceptual equivalence with the original and adjusted the wording; (c) a focus group of 10 participants commented on item clarity and comprehensibility; (d) four external expert judges rated each item (see below); and (e) the same two authors revised the items according to the judges' ratings and comments, which produced the final version.
No independent back-translation was carried out.
Additional details are given in the online supplemental material.
Intuitive Eating Scale-2 (Tylka & Kroon Van Diest, 2013) assesses how much individuals regulate their eating based on internal hunger and satiety cues rather than external rules or emotional factors.
text.formatted: Intuitive Eating Scale-2 (Tylka & Kroon Van Diest, 2013) assesses how much individuals regulate their eating based on internal hunger and satiety cues rather than external rules or emotional factors.

text.text: The scale comprises four dimensions: Unconditional Permission to Eat, Eating for Physical Rather than Emotional Reasons, Reliance on Hunger and Satiety Cues, and Body-Food Choice Congruence.
Items are rated on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree), with higher scores indicating greater intuitive eating.
Internal consistency of the Spanish version (Flores-Quijano et al., 2023) demonstrated good reliability in this sample.
Participants were recruited through announcements disseminated on various social media platforms, including WhatsApp, Instagram, LinkedIn, and Reddit.
Data were collected using SurveyMars, an online survey platform, through its free version.

SurveyMars complies with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and implements data protection measures such as encrypting data at rest and in transit, access controls, and secure data storage in accordance with European data protection standards (SurveyMars, n.d.).

To address optimism, we computed bootstrap 95% CIs (2,000 resamples) for the AUC and the cutoff, and 10-fold stratified cross-validated sensitivity and specificity (100 repetitions), deriving the cutoff only from the training folds.
Incremental validity.

A hierarchical regression predicted BES total scores in three blocks: age and BMI (Block 1); uncontrolled eating and emotional eating (TFEQ) and the HEDO-Q total score (Block 2); and the PFS total score (Block 3).
The unique contribution of the PFS was evaluated using the change in R² and the F change at Block 3.
Sociodemographic and hunger-related analyses.

We examined associations of PFS scores with age, biological sex, BMI, educational level, dieting status, and hormonal cycle category using correlations or group comparisons, depending on the variable type.

Linear regression tested whether PFS scores predicted post-exposure hunger controlling for baseline hunger and BMI, and an interaction model tested whether this association varied with baseline hunger.
Associations among PFS scores, BES scores, and the HEDO-Q dimensions were examined to describe a hedonic profile.
